title: The Consul's Son: a Cadiz-born Norwegian who built the face of Buenos Aires
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Cadiz, the consul's son is born
stops.date_confidence: attested; day, month and year all given
stops.campa: In a port that has been dispatching ships to the Rio de la Plata for three centuries, a son is born to Otto Thorvald Alexander Christophersen, Norwegian consul in Spain, and to Fanny Younger. The boy holds Spain by birth and Norway by blood, and will carry both to the end of his life. Cadiz teaches his eye its first grammar: white stucco under salt light, a cathedral dome riding over low streets, everything facing water. No record names the house he is born in. The city stands in for it.
suggested_refs: The Norwegian consulate at Cadiz in the 1860s, held by Thorvald Christophersen

stops.name: Kristiania, sent north to his father's country
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1. The city is a proxy: sources say only that he was sent to Norway, naming neither town nor school
stops.campa: At eleven he is put on a ship going the wrong way, north instead of west, to be schooled in the country his father left. Norwegian becomes a language he owns rather than inherits. The record of these years is one clause long: he studies in Norway. No town, no school, no teacher, no holiday. He will build a church for Norwegian sailors in Buenos Aires forty years later and a bank for Scandinavian money the year after that, which is the only evidence anyone has of what the north put into him.
suggested_refs: Norwegian secondary schooling in the 1870s and 1880s; no register naming Christophersen has been located

stops.name: Brussels, architecture and scenography
stops.date_confidence: graduation year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: He takes his degree from the School of Architecture and Scenography at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Brussels. The school's own name yokes the two trades together, and he never quite separates them: a facade is a wall, and it is also the flat behind which a family performs its rank. Belgium gives him more than the diploma. Twenty years on, a Belgian mortgage bank looking for a Buenos Aires house will come to the Argentine architect who read his first orders in Brussels.
suggested_refs: The Escuela de Arquitectura y Escenografia of the Academie royale des Beaux-Arts, Brussels

stops.name: Paris, the Beaux-Arts finishing
stops.date_confidence: no dates whatever are given for the Paris period; placed after the 1885 Brussels graduation by sequence alone. The atelier of Jean-Louis Pascal is reported but not attested in the cited articles
stops.campa: After Brussels comes Paris and the Ecole des Beaux-Arts, where the discipline he will practise for fifty years is codified: axis, hierarchy, the plan that reads like a sentence, ornament as argument rather than decoration. The sources give him no arrival and no departure. What he learns here he will unload at the mouth of a river six thousand miles away, onto families who want their money to look like the seventeenth century. A generation later, young men in Buenos Aires will call this training the enemy.
suggested_refs: The Ecole des Beaux-Arts, Paris, and the academic doctrine exported to the Rio de la Plata

stops.name: Montevideo, first landfall in the south
stops.date_confidence: year per es.wiki; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1. The English article instead dates his arrival in the region to 1888, and the two accounts may be one crossing counted twice
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic in his twenty-first year and comes ashore first on the Uruguayan side, in a city that is a smaller rehearsal of the one waiting across the water. Nothing is recorded of the stay: no address, no work, no reason for stopping here rather than going on. He will return to Montevideo twice as an architect, in 1907 and in 1924, to build houses for men named Urtubey and Morato. The first of the two will be pulled down; so will the beginning of his own record here.
suggested_refs: The Ciudad Vieja and the port of Montevideo in the late 1880s

stops.name: Buenos Aires, off the ship at the Darsena Norte
stops.date_confidence: year per en.wiki; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1. Contradiction with the 1887 Uruguay landing is left standing. The landing point is reconstructed: 1880s transatlantic passengers came ashore at the Darsena Norte, by the Hotel de Inmigrantes
stops.campa: He walks off a ship into a city with money, no skyline, and an appetite for looking European. Buenos Aires in 1888 is knocking down its colonial blocks as fast as the wheat trade pays for it, and importing architects the way it imports iron. He is twenty-two, holds a Brussels degree and a Paris polish, and speaks Spanish, French and Norwegian. He will not leave again except to work. Fifty-eight years later he is buried eleven blocks from where he lands.
suggested_refs: The Darsena Norte and the immigrant landing stage of 1880s Buenos Aires

stops.name: Belgrano, the last house with Kihlberg
stops.date_confidence: es.wiki dates the house c. 1892; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1. The start year of the Kihlberg partnership is nowhere attested; only its close in 1892 is
stops.campa: His first years in Argentina are spent in partnership with a Swede, Carl Kihlberg, two northerners drawing for a Latin city. Together they raise a railway station for the Ferrocarril Bahia Blanca al Noroeste and, in the leafy blocks of Belgrano, a residence for Nicholas Bouwer on Juramento. When the partnership dissolves in 1892 the Bouwer house is among the last things with two names on it. Everything he builds after this carries one, and there will be more than a working lifetime of it.
suggested_refs: The Nicholas Bouwer residence, Juramento 1938, Belgrano, with Carl Kihlberg

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the studio opens alone
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to a mid-year placeholder after the close of the Kihlberg partnership
stops.campa: At twenty-six he sets up on his own account, and the practice he opens will run for close to fifty years without interruption: hospitals, banks, churches, schools, pantheons, palaces, an exchange, a stock of provincial branch offices, and the private houses of families who name themselves in the plan. He works for Catholics, for Russian Orthodox, for Spanish mutual aid societies, for Norwegian sailors and Belgian bankers. The city he arrived in as a foreigner becomes, block by block, a thing he has written.
suggested_refs: The independent practice of Alejandro Christophersen, 1892 to about 1941

segments.name: Avenida de Mayo and the First Decade Alone

stops.name: Gallo 1330, the children's hospital
stops.date_confidence: build years 1893-1896 attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: The first large public thing he builds is a hospital for children, raised between 1893 and 1896 on Gallo street and named for Ricardo Gutierrez. It opens its doors in 1896 and has not stopped working since. The commission arrives in the same season as a cafe facade and a rented palace on the new boulevard, so the record refuses the tidy story in which a career begins with one building. Three jobs begin it at once, and only this one is still full of people every morning.
suggested_refs: The Hospital de Ninos Dr. Ricardo Gutierrez, Gallo 1330, opened 1896
sources: Wikipedia (es): Hospital de Ninos Ricardo Gutierrez

stops.name: Flores, a public school on Fray Cayetano Rodriguez
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: Between the hospital and the boulevard he builds a state primary school in Flores, out where the city is still becoming itself, and it is given the name of Leandro N. Alem. It is a small job in a list that will fill with palaces, and one of very few he does for the education of children who are not the children of clients. The works list gives it a line and a number, Escuela 19, and nothing else: no photograph, no description, no note of whether it stands.
suggested_refs: Escuela No. 19 Leandro N. Alem, Fray Cayetano Rodriguez 95, Flores

stops.name: Mar del Plata, a chalet by the sea for Leloir
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the demolished-works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: The families he builds for in town go south to the sea in summer, and they want the summer house to say what the town house says. On Alvear street in the Lomas de Stella Maris he raises a chalet for Antonio Leloir, in the first wave of the resort city's building fever. It is his earliest work outside greater Buenos Aires and one of the earliest to be lost: the chalet is demolished, and the works list records it only under the heading of things that no longer stand.
suggested_refs: The Antonio Leloir chalet, Alvear 2010, Mar del Plata, demolished

stops.name: Avenida de Mayo 825, a new front for the Tortoni
stops.date_confidence: the Cafe Tortoni article dates the facade 1898; the biography's works list dates the Unzue job 1893. Contradiction left open. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: Cutting the Avenida de Mayo through the old grid tears the front off Saturnino Unzue's house and leaves the building facing a boulevard it was never designed for. Christophersen gives it a new French academic face and lets the old Rivadavia entrance survive as a back door. Behind that facade the Cafe Tortoni goes on pouring coffee, and it is still pouring it, listed among the city's protected bars. He also builds two doors along, at number 902, for Maria Carranza de Lawson.
suggested_refs: The Cafe Tortoni facade, Av. de Mayo 825; the Carranza de Lawson building at Av. de Mayo 902, later the Hotel Astoria

stops.name: Chacarita, the pantheon of the Spanish society
stops.date_confidence: the works list gives 1898 flat; a Wikimedia Commons file caption gives 1896-1898. Month and day unknown, defaulted to a mid-year placeholder
stops.campa: The Spanish Mutual Aid Society, burying its members in a city that is half immigrant, commissions a pantheon in the Chacarita cemetery, and gets from him a neo-baroque house for the dead. He is Spanish himself by birth and by passport, one of the hundreds of thousands the peninsula sent across, and this is the first of several commissions in which a community that has crossed water asks him to give its foreignness an address. He will build for the Russians next, then for the Norwegians.
suggested_refs: The Panteon de la Sociedad Espanola de Socorros Mutuos, Cementerio de la Chacarita
sources: Wikimedia Commons: Cementerio de La Chacarita 04.JPG

stops.name: Avenida Brasil 315, the Russian church
stops.date_confidence: begun 1898, built and adapted by 1901 per the cathedral's own article; the English biography's 1905 is contradicted by that article. Month and day unknown, defaulted to a placeholder in the year of the start
stops.campa: Five onion domes come up across from Parque Lezama for the Orthodox congregation of a diplomatic and emigre community. The design arrives from Saint Petersburg, from Mihail Preobrazhensky of the Holy Synod, and Christophersen adapts it to the ground and the trade of Buenos Aires with the engineer Pedro Coni. Work begins in 1898 and the church is finished in 1901, opened with the president of the republic present. He signs it as an adapter, not an author, and it is among the most recognizable things he touches.
suggested_refs: The Catedral de la Santisima Trinidad, Av. Brasil 315, after Mihail Preobrazhensky
sources: Wikipedia (es): Catedral de la Santisima Trinidad

segments.name: The Profession, and the Banks of the Interior

stops.name: Buenos Aires, founding a school for the trade
stops.date_confidence: no source gives any year for the founding; the date is a sequence placeholder only and must not be read as attested. The often-quoted 1900 is equally unsupported
stops.campa: With Paul Hary and Joaquin Mariano Belgrano he founds a school of architecture for a country that has been importing its architects, and he takes a titular chair in it, under the Faculty of Exact and Natural Sciences of the University of Buenos Aires. He is also one of the refounders of the Sociedad Central de Arquitectos. A Norwegian account says he headed the architects' body several times; the Argentine one does not say it. No source anywhere gives a year for any of it.
suggested_refs: The founding of the Buenos Aires school of architecture with Paul Hary and Joaquin Mariano Belgrano

stops.name: Avenida Belgrano 2852, the Braceras house
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: A residence for the Braceras family goes up on Avenida Belgrano, and like most of the private houses he builds it does not stay a house. In time an association takes it over, and the works list records the new owner by four initials it never expands. What the letters stand for is written down nowhere that names them. The city does this to him repeatedly: a palace becomes a ministry, a bank becomes a court, and the family that ordered the plan survives as the old name of an address.
suggested_refs: The Braceras residence, Av. Belgrano 2852, later occupied by the AFCP

stops.name: Bahia Blanca, a national bank at the port
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: Six hundred kilometres south, where the grain of the pampas is loaded onto ships, he builds a branch of the Banco de la Nacion Argentina on Estomba street. The state bank is spreading through the country town by town, and it wants each of its houses to look like the same idea of solvency. The building outlives the use: it becomes the customs house of Bahia Blanca. He has been down this way before, drawing a station for the Bahia Blanca al Noroeste railway with Kihlberg.
suggested_refs: The Banco de la Nacion Argentina at Estomba 2, Bahia Blanca, later the Aduana

stops.name: Bartolome Mitre 226, the Belgian mortgage bank
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: The Sociedad Hipotecaria Belga America, lending Belgian money against Argentine land, builds its Buenos Aires house on Bartolome Mitre, and the architect it hires took his degree in Brussels. Whether the one fact produced the other is not written down anywhere; it sits in the record as a coincidence with a shape. In the same year he draws bank branches for three provincial towns at once, and the plan of a European bank downtown is not so different from the plan of a state bank on a dirt street.
suggested_refs: The Sociedad Hipotecaria Belga America, Bartolome Mitre 226

stops.name: Dolores, a bank on the corner of Belgrano and Rico
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to a mid-year placeholder. The coordinate is the town centre, the exact corner not confirmed
stops.campa: In the flat cattle country south of the capital he sets a Banco de la Nacion branch on the corner of Belgrano and General Rico. The same year he does the same thing at Chacabuco, on the corner of Belgrano and Sarmiento, out on the pampas to the west. These are the buildings that carry a Beaux-Arts education into towns of a few thousand souls, where the bank and the church are the only two facades with an order on them, and where his name is not attached to either in local memory.
suggested_refs: Banco de la Nacion Argentina branches at Dolores and at Chacabuco, both 1905

stops.name: Corrientes, the bank that becomes a courthouse
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to a placeholder. The coordinate is the Carlos Pellegrini and La Rioja corner as located today
stops.campa: The furthest north he builds is Corrientes, on the great river a thousand kilometres up from the estuary, at the corner of Carlos Pellegrini and La Rioja. It is another house for the national bank, in a subtropical city with its own century of Spanish and Guarani history behind it. Federal justice takes the building over later and hears cases in the rooms drawn for tellers and safes. He never lives anywhere but Buenos Aires; his drawings travel the length of the country without him.
suggested_refs: The former Banco de la Nacion at Carlos Pellegrini y La Rioja, Corrientes, later the federal courts

stops.name: Cerrito 1250, a house for Pedro Mendez
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: On Cerrito street, in the blocks behind what will be the opera house, he builds a private residence for Pedro Mendez. It belongs to the run of society houses that fills his middle years, each of them a French front on an Argentine fortune, each of them commissioned by a man who wants his surname legible from the pavement. The works list gives the client, the street and the year, and nothing more. What the house looked like inside is not recorded in anything reachable.
suggested_refs: The Pedro Mendez residence, Cerrito 1250

stops.name: Avenida Rivadavia 4879, the parish of Caacupe
stops.date_confidence: build years 1906-1909 attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to a mid-year placeholder in the start year
stops.campa: Out along Rivadavia, in Caballito, he builds a parish church under the title of Our Lady of Caacupe, the Virgin of Paraguay, for a neighbourhood filling with people from the north and from across the river. It takes three years. The churches run all through his career like a second practice beside the first: Orthodox in 1898, Catholic here, a sailors' chapel in 1918, a basilica in his sixties. The palaces make his name and the churches keep his hand in a plainer kind of work.
suggested_refs: The Parroquia Nuestra Senora de Caacupe, Av. Rivadavia 4879, Caballito

stops.name: Montevideo, the Urtubey house on Bulevar Artigas
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the demolished-works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1. The coordinate is the Avenida Rivera and Bulevar Artigas junction, the exact plot unrecorded
stops.campa: Twenty years after coming ashore here he returns to Montevideo as an architect and builds a residence for Ignacio de Urtubey where Avenida Rivera meets Bulevar Artigas. The two capitals of the estuary read each other's fashions across the water, and the men who commission houses in one often bank in the other. The Urtubey house is pulled down in due course, and so is the only other thing Uruguay ever asks him for. Both stand in the works list under the heading of the demolished, an eastern bank that hired him twice across forty years and kept nothing.
suggested_refs: The Ignacio de Urtubey residence, Av. Rivera and Bulevar Artigas, Montevideo, demolished

stops.name: Libertad 1264, the Leloir palace
stops.date_confidence: 1908 per the es.wiki works list; the English article dates the same house to 1903 and names its owner Adela Unzue de Leloir. Contradiction left open. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: On Libertad street, a block from the Plaza Lavalle, he raises the Leloir palace, and by the time anyone writes his biography the building is no longer called that. The Italian community's club takes it over in 1944 and the address becomes the Circulo Italiano, which is how the city knows it now. The two accounts of the house disagree by five years and by the first name of the client. What they agree on is that he built it and that the family that ordered it did not keep it.
suggested_refs: The former Palacio Leloir, Libertad 1264, seat of the Circulo Italiano since 1944

stops.name: Arenales 761, the Anchorena palace
stops.date_confidence: designed 1905, completed and inaugurated 1909 per the building's own article; the English article says 1910. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1. The circulating range 1909-1916 has no source and is not used here
stops.campa: Mercedes Castellanos de Anchorena wants one house on Plaza San Martin for three branches of her family, and she gets three palaces behind a single Parisian front, arranged around a court, drawn to be lived in and to be entered from a carriage. It is the largest private thing he ever builds and the thing his name is now attached to. The family holds it twenty-seven years. Then the state buys it, and the ballroom where an Anchorena received becomes the room where Argentina receives foreign ministers.
suggested_refs: The Palacio Anchorena, Arenales 761, Retiro, commissioned by Mercedes Castellanos de Anchorena

stops.name: Rosario, two houses on Cordoba street
stops.date_confidence: no date whatever is given for the Rosario houses; the year here is a sequence placeholder and is not attested. Coordinates from the street numbers, Cordoba 1814 and 1852
stops.campa: In Rosario, the grain port upriver, he builds two houses two doors apart on Cordoba street: one for Luis Pinasco, one for Casiano Casas and Adela Echesortu. Both outlive their families and both are taken by institutions, the first by the rectorate of the national university, the second by the college of notaries. The works list gives them no year at all, so the decade is guesswork and is admitted as guesswork. Two facades survive with better documentation than their own dates.
suggested_refs: The Pinasco house, Cordoba 1814, now the UNR rectorate; the Casas and Echesortu house, Cordoba 1852, now the Colegio de Escribanos
sources: Wikipedia (es): Alejandro Christophersen, works list, Rosario

stops.name: Cementerio El Salvador, the Rosario pantheons
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source; placed beside the Rosario houses by client identity, not by any attested year
stops.campa: The same Casiano Casas who commissions a house on Cordoba street commissions his tomb, and Christophersen builds both, the address for the living and the address after it. A second pantheon in the same cemetery, for Meliton Ibarlucea, is attributed to him too. It is a habit of his practice: the Spanish society at Chacarita, these two at El Salvador, and by one Norwegian account a number of vaults in Recoleta, where he himself will be laid without any source recording which stone is his.
suggested_refs: The Casiano Casas and Meliton Ibarlucea pantheons, Cementerio El Salvador, Rosario
sources: Wikipedia (es): Alejandro Christophersen, works list, Rosario

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the house of the composer Williams
stops.date_confidence: the only date is a critic's 'alrededor de 1910' written in 2016; month and day unknown, defaulted to a placeholder. The house is not located in the reachable sources and the coordinate is the city anchor
stops.campa: He builds a house for the family of the composer Alberto Williams, and a century later a critic looking at photographs of it calls it possibly the best architecture he ever made. The judgement is not one he ever hears. It is written in 2016, in an essay about the composer's son, the architect Amancio Williams, who will spend his own life proving that everything his father's generation built the wrong way round. The house is praised as an aside in an argument against it.
stops.quote: Esta casa pertenecio a su padre, el compositor Alberto Williams, y fue realizada por Alejandro Christophersen -posiblemente su mejor obra de arquitectura- alrededor de 1910.
stops.quote_source: Alejandro Hernandez Galvez, 'La casa: el puente y el pasillo', Arquine, 19 February 2016; a critic's assessment written seventy years after Christophersen's death, not his own words
suggested_refs: Arquine, 'La casa: el puente y el pasillo', 19 February 2016, on the house of Alberto Williams

stops.name: Adolfo Alsina, the actors' house and the Dassen palace
stops.date_confidence: both dated 1914 in the works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1. The Palacio Dassen is given only as 'Adolfo Alsina' with no number, so it shares this coordinate
stops.campa: In one year and on one street he builds two very different things: the headquarters of the Argentine Actors' Association, professional house of people who work at night, and the Palacio Dassen, drawn with Claro Cornelio Dassen himself. Adolfo Alsina runs through the old parish blocks behind the cathedral, and by 1914 he has three or four buildings standing on it. The works list gives the Dassen palace no street number at all, which is as much as anyone now knows about where it was.
suggested_refs: The Asociacion Argentina de Actores, Adolfo Alsina 1762; the Palacio Dassen, Adolfo Alsina, with Claro Cornelio Dassen

stops.name: Barracas, the Instituto del Buen Consejo
stops.date_confidence: build years 1914-1916 attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to a mid-year placeholder in the start year
stops.campa: While the exchange is going up downtown he builds a religious institute in Barracas, on Santa Maria del Buen Aire, in the working southern quarter by the Riachuelo. Two years of work, finished the year the Bolsa opens. Three commissions run at once out of the one studio in these years: the palace for a family, the exchange for a market, the institute for an order of sisters. Nobody who writes about him afterwards puts the three of them in the same sentence.
suggested_refs: The Instituto Nuestra Senora del Buen Consejo, Santa Maria del Buen Aire 953, Barracas

stops.name: Bolsa de Comercio, the exchange in Louis XVI dress
stops.date_confidence: designed 1913, inaugurated 1916, both attested; month and day of the inauguration unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: The stock exchange takes its third and grandest house from him, drawn in 1913 in Louis XVI dress with facades in simil-piedra Paris, and it opens in 1916 on the corner where Sarmiento meets the Bajo. Troiano Troiani cuts its sculptural decoration, working beside Riganti, an Italian's hands on a Norwegian's building for a market that prices the wheat of the pampas. The exchange's own account of itself names no sculptor. Half a century later a modernist tower is bolted on behind it.
suggested_refs: The Bolsa de Comercio de Buenos Aires, Sarmiento 299 and Av. L. N. Alem 356, inaugurated 1916
sources: Wikipedia (es): Bolsa de Comercio de Buenos Aires

stops.name: Ingeniero Huergo 1267, the church of the Norwegian sailors
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the demolished-works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: By the docks he builds a church for Norwegian seamen, the one commission in his life that answers the half of him that went north at eleven. Norway sends more of its men to sea than to anywhere else, and the ones who reach the Rio de la Plata want a room where the hymns are in their own language. The consul's son builds it for them. Later the city drives the Autopista 25 de Mayo through the block and the church comes down for the roadway, leaving one photograph and a line in a list.
suggested_refs: The Iglesia de los Marineros Noruegos, Av. Ing. Huergo 1267, demolished for the Autopista 25 de Mayo

stops.name: Sarmiento 354, the Scandinavian bank
stops.date_confidence: projected 1919, inaugurated 1920, both attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: A year after the sailors' church he draws the Buenos Aires house of the Banco Escandinavo Argentino on Sarmiento street, projected in 1919 and open in 1920. Two Nordic commissions back to back, the chapel and the counting house, one for the men on the ships and one for the money the ships carry. Neither stands today. The bank building is listed with the demolished, like the church, and the northern thread in his work survives only as two entries under a heading of things that are gone.
suggested_refs: The Banco Escandinavo Argentino, Sarmiento 354, projected 1919, demolished

stops.name: Serrano, a church and a college on the Cordoba plain
stops.date_confidence: completed by 1922 per the works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1. The coordinate is the town of Serrano, Departamento Presidente Roque Saenz Pena; the building footprint is not confirmed
stops.campa: Five hundred kilometres inland, in a Cordoba farming town on the plain, he builds a church of the Assumption and the college of San Alberto y San Enrique beside it. Serrano has a few thousand inhabitants and a grain elevator, and now it has an academic facade drawn by a man trained in Brussels and Paris who never, so far as any record shows, sets foot in the place. The works list gives the year and the two names. It gives no client, no cost, and no account of how a Cordoba parish five hundred kilometres away came to hire him.
suggested_refs: The Iglesia Asuncion de la Santisima Virgen and Colegio San Alberto y San Enrique, Serrano, Cordoba

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the Argentine pavilion
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to the month of the exposition's opening. The coordinate is the Esplanada do Castelo fairground area, not a confirmed pavilion footprint
stops.campa: Brazil marks a hundred years of independence with an international exposition on the reclaimed ground of the Esplanada do Castelo, and Argentina sends a pavilion drawn by Christophersen. It is the only time his work represents his adopted country abroad, and it is built to come down when the fair closes. He is fifty-six, and he does the job in plaster, for a crowd, in a language of facades that everyone at the fair reads fluently. Nothing of the pavilion survives. No photograph of it is named in the sources, and the works list carries it among the demolished with a year, a city, and no description at all.
suggested_refs: The Argentine pavilion at the Exposicao Internacional do Centenario, Rio de Janeiro, 1922

segments.name: The Quarrel with the New Century

stops.name: Montevideo, the Morato house at Carrasco
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the works list; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1. The street name is misspelled 'Alberbi' in the source
stops.campa: At fifty-eight he crosses the river once more for a house, this one for Ovidio Morato on the Avenida Juan B. Alberdi, out towards Carrasco. It is the last commission Uruguay gives him and the second of the two on the eastern bank. The works list misspells the street, which is a fair emblem of the state of his record: a man with two hundred buildings behind him whose entries are copied without checking, in a table with no citations and a scatter of wrong numbers.
suggested_refs: The Ovidio Morato residence, Av. Dr. Juan B. Alberdi 6189, Carrasco Norte, Montevideo

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the polemic with Virasoro
stops.date_confidence: the source gives only 'la decada del 1920'; no year, month or day is attested and the date here is a mid-decade placeholder. The commonly repeated 1925 is invented
stops.campa: Alejandro Virasoro builds in concrete without a cornice on it and says the ornament is a lie about the structure. Christophersen, sixty years old and holding a chair, answers in print for the academic tradition: proportion learned from the past, ornament as the argument a building makes about itself. The two of them carry it on through the decade in the professional press of a city that is simultaneously raising his basilica and Virasoro's art deco blocks. No source records who is thought to have won.
suggested_refs: The 1920s polemic between Christophersen and Alejandro Virasoro over academicism, rationalism and art deco

stops.name: Palermo Chico, the house on Cavia street
stops.date_confidence: the house is dated approximately 1927 by a commercial website and by no scholarly source; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: In Palermo Chico, where the newest money is building the newest French houses, a residence goes up on Cavia street that the city will one day protect by law as holding the very essence of the grand siecle, a balanced play of mass and light, synthetic and refined. It is a small building doing quietly what the Anchorena palace does at scale. A sentence about modern architecture is attributed to him from this house and from nowhere else, with no letter or article behind it.
stops.quote: El arte arquitectonico moderno no se deja atrapar por los detalles, sino que le da un giro nuevo a una idea antigua.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Christophersen on the Casa Cavia website (casa-cavia-ew1j.squarespace.com/la-casa), fetched and confirmed verbatim there; the site is a hospitality page and names no letter, article or memoir as its origin, so the attribution is unverified

sources: Proyecto de ley de catalogacion patrimonial, Gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, as quoted there

stops.name: Avenida Belgrano and Pasco, the basilica of Santa Rosa
stops.date_confidence: 1928-1934 per the basilica's own article and the English biography; the works list alone says 1926. Month and day of the start unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: In his sixties he builds the largest of his churches, the sanctuary of Santa Rosa de Lima, first saint of the Americas, on the corner of Avenida Belgrano and Pasco. Six years of work. It is inaugurated on the twelfth of October 1934 and blessed by Cardinal Pacelli, who will be pope within five years, and consecrated in 1941 on the ninth of his birthdays after that. Twelve years remain to him when the doors open, and the building outlasts the argument he is having about how to build.

stops.name: Avenida Avellaneda 2679, Regina Apostolorum
stops.date_confidence: completed by 1931 per the works list; the start year is not given, and month and day are unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: In Flores, a few blocks from the school he built for the state thirty-seven years earlier, he finishes the church of Regina Apostolorum. He is sixty-five. The neighbourhood he worked in as a young man with one hospital and one boulevard commission behind him now has his handwriting on it twice, at either end of a career, in a public school and a parish church. The works list gives the second one a single year and no beginning, as it does with most of the last decade.

stops.name: Arenales 761, the palace becomes the Palacio San Martin
stops.date_confidence: year of the state purchase attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1. The national monument declaration follows in 1994
stops.campa: The state buys the Anchorena palace and installs the Ministry of Foreign Relations and Worship in it, renaming it for San Martin. Christophersen is seventy and still working; he lives to see the largest house he built stop being a house. Ambassadors present credentials in the rooms he drew for a family of three branches. In 1994 the building is declared a national historic monument, which is the nearest thing to a monument in his own name that the record contains, and it does not carry his name.

stops.name: Avenida Corrientes 480, the Transradio building
stops.date_confidence: completed by 1940 per the works list; the start year is not given, and month and day are unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: At seventy-four he builds an office block on Avenida Corrientes for Transradio, the company that sends Argentine words across the ocean by wireless. A man trained before the telephone reached Buenos Aires draws the house of the radio. A bank takes the building over later. It is among the last things he finishes, in a downtown that has stopped commissioning the kind of facade he spent fifty years perfecting and has started building the towers his opponents drew in the twenties.

stops.name: Agronomia, the last commission
stops.date_confidence: completed by 1941 per the works list; the start year is not given, and month and day are unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: The last documented thing he builds is a school for the congregation of Santa Magdalena Sofia Barat, out on Salvador Maria del Carril in Agronomia, finished when he is seventy-five. Fifty-three years after coming off the ship, the practice closes with a building for teaching sisters on the edge of town, which is roughly where it began, with a hospital and a state primary school. Five years of life remain to him and no work in them is recorded anywhere.

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta, buried among his own vaults
stops.date_confidence: attested; day, month and year all given
stops.campa: He dies in Buenos Aires on the fourth of February 1946, seventy-nine years old, holding Argentine and Spanish papers, and is buried in the Recoleta, the aristocratic necropolis in the quarter he spent decades building for. A Norwegian account says he was the architect of a number of the vaults in it. Not one of them is named, and neither is his. No cause of death is recorded, no address where he died, no wife, no children. The city he wrote across keeps no stone that says which of them is his.
suggested_refs: The Cementerio de la Recoleta, where Christophersen built vaults for others and lies in an unlocated one himself
